source.title: When and how epochwise double descent happens

record.tranche_reason: The authors explicitly say they replicated the experimental setup of the original deep double-descent study, then report epochwise test-error results for ResNet18 on CIFAR10 across widths and label-noise levels.
record.gate_note: The study also cites prior results and uses hyperparameter sweeps to select settings; those cited results and selection-only values are not recorded as rows. Rows below cover the study's own theoretical analysis and experiments.
record.test_reason: Section 5 replicates the Nakkiran et al. ResNet18/CIFAR10 setup with SGD and their hyperparameters. It sweeps width (k=4–92) and label noise (ε=0–0.1) and reports test error over epochs, which directly tests V2 and the noise dependence in V6. Sections 7–8 argue explicitly that a final-layer-converged procedure is a counterexample to the EMC hypothesis (V5), giving T5-type content as well.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that EDD needs both overparameterization and label noise above a critical threshold. Above a second, higher threshold, early stopping beats training to convergence. They attribute EDD to informative but slow-to-learn features interacting with label noise, not to EMC, and call the final-layer procedure a strict counterexample to the EMC hypothesis. Of their two removal methods, PCA truncation hurts accuracy, while the converged final layer matches or beats standard training.
record.recipe_differences: The authors replicated the prior ResNet18/CIFAR10 setup but varied label-noise levels and network widths; they did not repeat the CIFAR100 experiments. Their linear-model analysis and final-layer replacement procedure are additional methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The observed epochwise behavior changes with network width, label-noise fraction, parameterization in the linear model, retaining or removing smaller principal components, and replacing the final layer with converged weights.

fits_no_version.finding: Above a second critical noise level (ε=0.1 at k=64/92), EDD occurs but the first minimum beats the final one, so early stopping is optimal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether the second descent is practically relevant (beats early stopping) depends on noise falling within an intermediate window.

record.problems: The deep-network experiments use ResNet18 on CIFAR10 only and average 10 random seeds. The paper notes that the ε = 0.025 peak is comparable to SGD jitter. The reported test-error values in the figures are not given numerically in the text, and the authors could not test whether much larger ResNet18 widths stop showing epochwise double descent.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results omitted. Figure 2 reports early-stopping versus convergence surfaces for the analytic model, but its summarized phase outcomes are represented by r1–r4 rather than separate figure-only rows.

untested.parts: Widths vary, but test error at convergence as a function of model size is not reported for ResNet18.
No model-wise curve across model classes; only the linear model's convergence error over λ (Fig. 2A) is shown, as theory.
EMC is never measured; the peak location relative to the interpolation epoch is not compared to an EMC prediction.
Multiple or triple peaks and removal under optimally tuned explicit regularization are not tested. Early stopping beating convergence at high noise is the only regularization-like result.

missing.what: Standard-training EDD curves at higher noise levels (ε up to 0.4) shown alongside the converged procedure; only the converged outcome is rowed.
Linear model generalization error at convergence across λ (model-wise curve) and the early-stopping-vs-convergence difference surfaces.
The prediction that very wide networks stop showing EDD, which the authors could not observe in ResNet18 at the widths they tested.

record.verdict_notes: Single architecture and dataset (ResNet18/CIFAR10), 10 seeds, no numeric values in the text. Section 5 uses the Nakkiran hyperparameters, which the authors found suboptimal; Sections 6–7 use swept hyperparameters, so r16 and r18 are not directly comparable to r5–r15. Figure and section numbering and the noise level in Section 6 are internally inconsistent. The linear-model rows derive from a noise model built to produce EDD, so they should not carry weight on their own. Preprint.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies network width but does not report test error at convergence as a function of model size.
The deep-network experiments are limited to ResNet18 on CIFAR10; they do not test other architectures, datasets, or training procedures.
No sweep of training-sample count near an interpolation threshold is reported.
The study does not test a general model-wise double-descent curve across model classes.
The counterexample is a particular final-layer training procedure on ResNet18; other definitions of effective complexity and other procedures are not tested.
The study varies label-noise level and reports noise-dependent epochwise behavior. It does not test multiple or triple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The study does not re-count parameters using an effective parameter measure or test whether that produces an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.check: Noise level is inconsistent in the source: the Section 6 text says ε=0.1, the Figure 4 caption says ε=0.2. Figure numbering in the text (Fig. 6) also mismatches the captions (Fig. 4). rows.subject: ResNet18 standard training
rows.operation_detail: Measured the standard training test-error trajectory for comparison with final-layer convergence.
rows.value: Standard training and final-layer-converged performance are equivalent within differences smaller than variation across random seeds.
rows.uncertainty: Mean ± standard deviation across 10 random seeds; numerical values not stated

rows.subject: ResNet18 with final classification layer replaced by converged weights
rows.stage_stated: earlier layers trained with SGD; final layer replaced using the analytic converged-weight solution
rows.operation_detail: After training for t epochs, replaced the final classification-layer weights with the analytic converged weights calculated from penultimate-layer activations.
rows.value: The final-layer-converged procedure eliminates epochwise double descent in all tested cases; for ε > 0 it also gives lower test error than standard training.
rows.uncertainty: Mean ± standard deviation across 10 random seeds; numerical values not stated
rows.note: The authors describe this procedure as a counterexample to the EMC hypothesis: the training procedure does not show epochwise double descent even as the number of samples fit with error ≤ const. exceeds the training-set size.
rows.check: Training-procedure intervention (analytic final-layer weights), with swept hyperparameters rather than the Section 5 setup. The V5 counterexample rests on the authors' assertion that EMC still exceeds n; neither EMC nor training error under this procedure is reported.

relation.reason: The study directly measures epochwise double descent under width and noise sweeps, tests interventions, and presents an explicit argument against the EMC explanation.

tranche.reason: Section 5 explicitly replicates the prior ResNet18/CIFAR10 setup and measures test error over epochs; Section 9.7 says it uses the prior work's hyperparameters. The additional theory and interventions do not remove this replication component.

source_check.notes: The PCA noise level is internally inconsistent: ε=0.1 in Section 6 versus ε=0.2 in Figure 4. Sections 6–7 use swept hyperparameters; the analytic readout uses the smooth-label approximation, and the EMC counterexample is asserted without measuring EMC.

statements.correction: Section 5: no EDD below ε=0.025 at any tested width, including k=64 and k=92. Section 7: analytic final-layer replacement at k=64 eliminates EDD. Section 8: authors assert that the modified procedure fits beyond the training-set size; EMC is not measured.
statements.problem: The low-noise absence is supported, but the text does not establish that those particular standard-SGD runs reached interpolation. The assertion about fitting beyond sample count concerns the final-layer intervention.
